Randolph.metaDescription: Raccoons, bats, squirrels, and woodchucks in Randolph, VT — village homes, Randolph Center farmhouses, and White River valley farms. Same-day service — call us today.
Randolph.housing_era: A three-village town — Randolph Village, Randolph Center, and East Randolph — with older village and college-area homes, classic hill farmhouses in the Center, and farms along the Third Branch of the White River.

Randolph.wildlife_intro:
Randolph's wildlife follows its farms and its older village housing. Bats roost in village attics and big Center barns, raccoons work feed rooms and chimneys, and woodchucks and skunks are constants on the hill farms. Squirrels — gray in the village, red in the woods — are the most common house call, and the Third Branch brooks give beavers places to flood the occasional field road and culvert.

Long winters make fall the proofing season in Randolph, and spring mud season the denning season, when our crew is busiest with raccoons and skunks under buildings. Bat exclusions are timed for spring or late August through November with one-way doors, winter is for sealing empty attics, and no colony work happens while pups cannot fly. Call us in fall and most of Randolph's winter calls never happen.

faqs.a: It depends on the species, how the animal got in, and how much proofing or cleanup the building needs, so we do not quote a firm price before seeing the job. faqs.q: Why are woodchucks such a fixture on Randolph farms?
faqs.a: Hill farms offer exactly what woodchucks want — dry banks, stone walls, and barn foundations to burrow under, with hay and gardens to eat. Removing the animal matters, but so does blocking the burrow entrance at the building with buried mesh. Our crew does both, which is why our woodchuck work holds.

Woodchucks work the intervale fields, beavers dam the valley brooks, and porcupines trouble the wooded homes below Wright's Mountain.

The valley's milder winters do not spare Bradford the fall rush — mice and squirrels still pour in before the cold, and our crew proofs village homes and farmhouses every autumn. Williamstown.wildlife_intro:
Williamstown's steep Gulf and hill farms give wildlife plenty of cover close to homes. Squirrels and bats are the main village calls, raccoons and skunks work the Gulf farms, and porcupines are a steady problem at camps and outbuildings in the woods around Limehurst Lake and the back roads. Woodchucks dig under barns across town, and beavers occasionally back water up on the Stevens Branch headwater brooks.

Fall in Williamstown means getting homes and camps sealed before snow closes the back roads, and our crew schedules that proofing early. Bat work is exclusion only — one-way doors in spring and late August through fall, full proofing from December through March, and no colony work while pups cannot fly. Mud season brings skunks and raccoons out with young, so call us at the first sign of a den under a building.

faqs.q: What damage do porcupines do around Williamstown camps?

Chelsea.wildlife_intro:
Chelsea's preserved village is beautiful, and its 1800s homes are exactly the buildings bats, squirrels, and raccoons prefer — tall attics, old chimneys, and small gaps that open with age. Down the First Branch valley, farms add barn raccoons, skunks, rats around feed, and woodchucks in the fields. The surrounding hills keep porcupines and red squirrels close to the rural homes and camps.

Historic fabric needs gentle, thorough work, and our crew proofs Chelsea homes without tearing into original trim — sealing every gap, fitting one-way doors for bats in spring or late August through fall, and finishing proofing in winter when colonies are away. No colony work happens while pups are flightless. Fall is the time to call, before mice and squirrels settle into those tall attics for a long valley winter.

faqs.q: How do you proof a historic Chelsea home without damaging it?

Our crew walks the whole roofline first, so the work is complete in one visit and the house keeps its character.

Tunbridge.wildlife_intro:
Tunbridge is dairy and hill-farm country, and its calls start with barns: raccoons, skunks, and rats around feed, bats in barn lofts and farmhouse attics, and woodchucks under outbuildings on nearly every farm. The villages add squirrels and chimney raccoons in older homes, and the ridge camps and homes see porcupines and red squirrels through the winter woods season.

Our crew works Tunbridge on the farm calendar — proofing in fall, denning calls in mud season, and bat exclusions timed for spring or late August through November with one-way doors. Winter is for sealing empty barns and attics, never for trapping a colony in, and no bat work happens while pups cannot fly. Compensated trapping here requires a valid Vermont trapping license, and our crew works under one — just ask when you call.

faqs.a: It depends on the species, how the animal got in, and how much proofing or cleanup the building needs, so we do not quote a firm price before seeing the job. faqs.q: Why do Tunbridge barns attract so many different animals?
faqs.a: A barn concentrates feed, water, shelter, and warmth in one building, and each species takes its share — raccoons and rats at the feed, bats in the loft, skunks under the floor. Our crew tackles the building as a whole: removing the animals present and closing the accesses each species uses, so the barn stays quiet.
